workItems.title: Remove repeated rules, unrelated branches and unasked navigation

cases.question: Is the filing ready for an LOC request under the guide's listed prerequisites?
cases.scenario: The filing does not require an initial or amended Certificate of Occupancy. Its status is Permit Entire; final PW3 costs are verified; all required documents are submitted; applicable final technical reports are certified; all permits are inspected and Signed-Off; and all AHV permits are approved.

findings.notes: Yes on the supplied listed prerequisites and owner/AOR Request LOC action are delivered. The answer distinguishes request readiness from approval but could explicitly qualify it on the current live record and unresolved items. Repeats the final PW3 detail unnecessarily.

cases.title: High-pressure natural gas piping
cases.question: A new natural-gas piping system in a Manhattan commercial building will operate at 15 psig. Can it be designed only under the ordinary Fuel Gas Code piping provisions, without considering Appendix G?

findings.reviewNote: The Appendix G conclusion at exactly 15 psig is correct. The answer adds interior-pressure, testing and appliance-flow checks that are unnecessary to that threshold decision, and contains the malformed word installation[]. Retained conversation facts incorrectly turn a new piping system in a commercial building into a new-construction building; the same error reproduces in the current local fact extractor.

cases.title: Gas appliance in a bathroom
cases.question: A designer wants to install a gas-fired appliance in a bathroom. Is a gas appliance categorically prohibited in every bathroom?

findings.finding: The general prohibition and exceptions remain; the sleeping-room installer and detector discussion is gone. Still repeats verification conditions. Minor precision improvement remains: exception 3 should refer to a door equipped with an approved self-closing device, preserving what the approval modifies.

cases.title: Large appliance using indoor combustion air
cases.question: A mechanical room contains gas appliances with a combined input of 400,000 Btu/h. The room is large enough to satisfy an indoor-air volume calculation. Can the designer rely entirely on indoor combustion air?

findings.reviewNote: Correctly distinguishes combined input from the individual-appliance threshold and requests the individual ratings. The first draft incorrectly applied an aggregate threshold; verification caused a successful repair. The closing outdoor-opening/DEP discussion is peripheral.

cases.title: Concealed gas-piping union
cases.question: A contractor proposes a union in a concealed gas-piping location above a permanent gypsum ceiling so the piping can be assembled more easily. Is that fitting permitted to remain concealed?

findings.reviewNote: Correct concealed-union conclusion, permitted fitting list, and accessible-location distinction. The separate appliance-union distance is not needed for the supplied facts.

cases.title: Operating gas piping before required testing
cases.question: A new gas-piping installation appears complete and leak-free. May the contractor place it in service before the required inspection and pressure test are completed?

findings.reviewNote: The answer clearly rejects appearance as a substitute for testing, preserves pre-service gas-tight testing and inspection/pressure testing before acceptance and initial operation, and binds both requirements to FGC 404.20 and 406.1. Missing test-procedure details are bounded without asking unnecessary facts.

cases.title: Minimum pressure test for a 2-psig system
cases.question: A gas system has a proposed maximum working pressure of 2 psig. The contractor proposes to test it at 2 psig because that equals the operating pressure. Is that test pressure sufficient?

findings.reviewNote: The ordinary 1.5 times 2 = 3 psig result and the separate higher/special testing conditions are supported. The answer keeps ordinary test duration unresolved. The general measurement procedure, repeated special-case checklist and supporting-point duplication can be shortened without deleting material exceptions.

cases.title: Gas piping in a public corridor
cases.question: New gas piping is installed in a public corridor. The contractor proposes a 5-psig pressure test for 30 minutes. Is that sufficient?

findings.reviewNote: The 10-psig/30-minute corridor result is supported. The response broadens into whether the corridor installation is permitted and asks for plans proving an installation exception, although the asked comparison concerns test pressure. Retain a bounded installation qualification without turning this into a general installation-readiness checklist.

cases.title: Using a valve as a pressure-test bulkhead
cases.question: Can an ordinary shutoff valve be used as the sole bulkhead between a gas-filled portion of a piping system and an adjacent portion being pressure tested?

findings.reviewNote: The single-valve prohibition, double-block-and-bleed/flange exception and section-test safeguards match the supplied provision. A second paragraph repeats general pre-service testing and inspection rules, and four supporting points prolong this narrow bulkhead answer.

cases.title: Supporting gas piping from another pipe
cases.question: A short run of gas piping is strapped to a nearby domestic-water pipe because there is no convenient structural support above. Is that acceptable if the water pipe is strong enough?

findings.reviewNote: The prohibition on supporting gas piping by other piping directly answers the stated water-pipe arrangement and is correctly cited. Detailed support standards, spacing and a request for MSS SP-58/Section 415 expand the answer beyond that resolved prohibition.

cases.title: Appliance shutoff valve eight feet away
cases.question: A gas appliance has a manual shutoff valve in the same room, eight feet from the appliance. There is no special manifold arrangement. Does the valve satisfy the ordinary appliance shutoff requirement?

findings.reviewNote: The ordinary six-foot limit, two-foot shortfall and valve installation conditions are supported. The remote-valve alternative remains conditional and cites its separate authority. Condense the alternative and follow-up checklist so the ordinary-distance question remains the focus.

cases.title: Appliance shutoff valve mounted 72 inches high
cases.question: The gas connection to a floor-mounted appliance is 30 inches above the floor, but the shutoff valve is mounted 72 inches above the floor. Is that acceptable under the ordinary shutoff-valve location rule?

findings.note: A 72-inch valve distance exceeds the 60-inch rule and the stated 30-inch connection does not qualify for the high-connection exception.

cases.title: Appliance supplied at pressure above its design pressure
cases.question: A gas appliance is designed for a lower inlet pressure than the pressure supplied by the building gas system. Can the appliance simply be connected directly if the connecting pipe is rated for the higher pressure?

findings.note: The line-pressure-regulator conclusion is correct after a rewrite. The missing-facts list still requests manufacturer pressure/instructions for a separate overpressure path that the answer says is not needed for the asked decision.

cases.title: Flexible connector to a water heater
cases.question: A contractor proposes a listed flexible gas connector between the branch piping and a gas-fired water heater. The connector is less than six feet long and is in the same room. Is it permitted?

findings.reviewNote: The answer applies the specific rigid-piping requirement to the water heater, explains why listing, same-room location and length do not override it, and binds the general connector comparison to the same section. It does not ask the user to reconfirm the supplied appliance type or dimensions.

cases.title: Commercial range on casters without restraint
cases.question: A commercial cooking appliance on casters is connected with a listed commercial gas connector, but no separate restraining device is provided. Is the listed connector alone sufficient?

findings.note: Listed connector for the movable appliance and a separate movement restraint are required.

cases.title: Type 1 gas clothes dryer and the meaning of “not required to be vented”
cases.question: FGC 501.8 lists a Type 1 clothes dryer among appliances not required to be vented. Does that mean a gas clothes dryer may discharge its dryer exhaust into the room?

findings.note: The final revised answer correctly separates dryer exhaust from the combustion-product venting chapter and requires outdoor discharge under MC 504.4. The rejected initial draft remains recorded.

cases.title: Air-conditioned office relying only on operable windows
cases.question: A new office has large operable windows that appear to provide enough natural ventilation. The office will also be fully air-conditioned. Can the design rely only on the operable windows for code-required ventilation?

findings.note: Mechanical ventilation is required for the stated air-conditioned office. The corrected draft binds the habitable-space definition and omits the unsupported assertion that windows may remain. Optional airflow rates make the narrow answer longer than necessary.

cases.title: Outdoor-air intake six feet from a side lot line
cases.question: On a 40-foot-wide zoning lot, a ventilation air intake is proposed six feet from an interior side lot line. Does that satisfy the ordinary Mechanical Code intake-location rule?

findings.reviewNote: The answer correctly applies the ordinary ten-foot lot-line distance, four-foot shortfall and under-twenty-foot lot exception. It also preserves the supplied Group R-3 exception without assuming occupancy. Other intake distances are explicitly outside this limited comparison; they do not undo the direct result.

cases.title: Recirculating ventilation air between apartments
cases.question: A central system serving two dwelling units is designed to use return air from Apartment A as part of the ventilation air supplied to Apartment B. Is that permitted?

findings.reviewNote: The cross-dwelling recirculation prohibition is correctly applied. The collateral transfer-air summary omits the source restriction where recirculation from the source is prohibited, and only/listed-types wording is stronger than the illustrative allowance. The saved and current fact extractor also demote the stated two dwelling units to unknown because the system is designed to use return air. The answer itself still gives the correct cross-unit No.

cases.title: Transfer air used as toilet-room makeup air
cases.question: Can conditioned air transferred from an adjacent occupied office be used as makeup air for a mechanically exhausted toilet room?

findings.reviewNote: The conditional transfer-air allowance and public-toilet exhaust rates are present. The response imports the recirculation rule into transfer-air reasoning and asks for air available after accounting for required office outdoor air, although its cited transfer-air provision permits required outdoor air to be introduced into the source occupied space. This creates a material ambiguity about transfer versus recirculation; clarify from the governing source before acceptance. Public/private fixture-count detail is also beyond the narrow permission question.

cases.title: Fan disconnect used as emergency ventilation control
cases.question: The only way to stop a building’s supply and return fans in an emergency is to operate the electrical disconnect at each fan. Does that satisfy the Mechanical Code’s manual ventilation-control requirement?

findings.reviewNote: The required manual emergency control, approved location and explicit disconnect-switch exclusion are correct. The main answer additionally cites MC 606.4.2 for automatic shutdown, but that reference has no returned citation or supporting point. It appears in retrieved-evidence metadata, so this is a returned citation/coverage gap, not proof that the source was never retrieved or that the underlying rule is false. Remove the unasked claim or bind its source.

cases.title: Mechanical ventilation of an uninhabited crawl space
cases.question: An uninhabited crawl space is not naturally ventilated. The designer proposes mechanical exhaust at 0.01 cfm per square foot that activates only when relative humidity reaches 70 percent. Is that enough?

findings.reviewNote: Correct exhaust and supply components, minimum airflow, humidity threshold, half-rate comparison, and later/higher proposed setpoint.

cases.title: Dryer exhaust combined with bathroom exhaust
cases.question: To reduce the number of exterior penetrations, a designer proposes combining a residential clothes-dryer exhaust duct with a bathroom exhaust duct before the air reaches the exterior. Is that permitted?

findings.reviewNote: The answer applies the independent dryer-exhaust rule directly, rejects combining the bathroom duct, and cites the outdoor dryer termination requirement. The environmental-air cross-reference is bounded and does not reopen the controlling independent-dryer result.

cases.title: Bathroom exhaust terminating in an attic
cases.question: A bathroom exhaust fan in a top-floor apartment discharges into a ventilated attic instead of directly outdoors. Is that acceptable because the attic itself has roof vents?

findings.reviewNote: The outdoor-discharge rule and express attic prohibition are correct, and the limited whole-house/private-attic exception is accurately distinguished from a bathroom fan. The exterior-location qualification remains conditional and does not treat attic roof vents as a compliant termination.

cases.title: Environmental exhaust four feet from an outdoor-air intake
cases.question: An environmental exhaust outlet is located four feet horizontally from a mechanical outdoor-air intake. No special exception or engineered re-entrainment analysis is identified. Is four feet enough?

findings.finding: The delivered answer reaches no/10 feet/6 feet short, correctly distinguishes the hazardous/noxious intake rule, and no longer invokes dining accessibility. Its compressed Class 1/Class 2 exception summary should distinguish the single-room Class 1 branch from the Class 2 dwelling/sleeping-unit branch. The recorded failed drafts contain this same grouping issue; eliminating their unrelated deterministic rejection does not certify their semantics.

cases.title: Apartment exhaust two feet from a neighboring apartment window
cases.question: In an R-2 building, a dedicated exhaust outlet serving one dwelling unit is two feet from an operable window serving the adjacent dwelling unit. Is that separation sufficient?

findings.reviewNote: The three-foot adjoining-unit minimum and one-foot shortfall are correct. The answer omits the reference distinction that two feet applies to an opening serving the same dwelling unit, despite having that source clause. It instead devotes the second paragraph to other outlet-location requirements.

cases.title: Screen on a clothes-dryer exhaust termination
cases.question: A contractor adds an insect screen over a clothes-dryer exhaust termination to prevent pests from entering the duct. Is the screen permitted?

findings.note: Dryer exhaust outlet screen is prohibited.

cases.title: Fire damper in a dryer exhaust duct
cases.question: A clothes-dryer exhaust duct crosses a fire-resistance-rated assembly. Can a listed fire damper be installed in the dryer duct to protect the penetration?

findings.note: Final revised answer correctly prohibits the fire/smoke damper and preserves rated-penetration protection. It contains unnecessary discussion of an unseen earlier duct-connection error.

cases.title: Type I hood over a medium-duty appliance
cases.question: A commercial kitchen appliance is classified as medium-duty cooking equipment and produces grease-laden vapors. Can it be installed under a Type II hood because the kitchen has only one appliance?

findings.finding: Correct Type I requirement for medium-duty grease-producing equipment, no one-appliance Type II allowance, and preserved tested-electric and listed integral down-draft alternatives. A bounded missing-fact repair removed unnecessary prerequisites and received a second semantic verification.

cases.title: Mixed appliances under one hood
cases.question: A single commercial kitchen hood serves several appliances. Most would ordinarily need only a Type II hood, but one appliance requires a Type I hood. Can the designer classify only the portion above that one appliance as Type I and treat the rest of the same hood as Type II?

findings.note: When any appliance under a single hood requires Type I, the entire hood must be Type I. Applicable listed recirculating-system qualification remains conditional.

cases.title: Kitchen makeup air not interlocked with exhaust
cases.question: A commercial kitchen has a mechanical makeup-air fan sized to offset the hood exhaust, but kitchen staff must switch the makeup-air fan on separately. Is that acceptable?

findings.finding: Correct automatic simultaneous operation and distinction from airflow sizing. The formerly unsupported approved-design-documents assertion is absent. The unasked intake-location discussion is supported but distracts from the controls decision. Energy Code coverage is explicitly unresolved.

cases.title: Using the 1968 Building Code for new plumbing and mechanical work
cases.question: An alteration is being designed under the optional 1968 Building Code provisions for a prior-code building. Does that election also allow new plumbing, fuel-gas, and mechanical work to be designed under the old technical requirements?

findings.reviewNote: The current technical-code exception to the optional 1968 Building Code election is correctly stated. The opening explanation introduces the separate pre-December-1968 law option without stating its multiple-dwelling/date scope there; the supporting point later provides those conditions. Keep the unasked historical path out of the lead or preserve its conditions at the claim. The fixture-count alternative and malformed bold spacing also lengthen the narrow answer.

cases.title: Assuming replacement equipment is automatically permit-exempt
cases.question: A contractor is replacing a piece of mechanical equipment with a similar new unit. Because the work is “replacement in kind,” can the contractor assume that no DOB permit is required?

findings.reviewNote: The answer correctly says replacement in kind alone does not establish an exemption and requests the actual replacement scope. It expands into emergency procedure and a one-year permit-denial consequence, then asks whether the equipment is connected to a building. Those additions distract from the particular exemption determination and add unnecessary missing facts.

cases.title: Permit-exempt work that violates zoning or another code
cases.question: A minor alteration qualifies for an exemption from the DOB permit requirement. Does that exemption also mean the work may disregard an otherwise applicable zoning or Construction Code requirement?

findings.finding: Correctly preserves substantive code, zoning and other-law compliance despite permit exemption. The answer unnecessarily revisits eligibility after the question already establishes it. No automatic web search occurred.

cases.title: Permit exemption and other agency approvals
cases.question: Work is exempt from a DOB permit under AC § 28-105.4. May the applicant also assume that filings or approvals otherwise required by another city, state, or federal agency are unnecessary?

findings.reviewNote: The answer correctly distinguishes the express other-City-agency language from the absence of any state/federal exemption. The deep-excavation DEC example is source-supported but unnecessary to this general independence question and adds a second repeated explanation.

cases.title: Occupied dwelling-unit information on a permit application
cases.question: A permit application covers work in an occupied residential building containing 20 dwelling units. The application does not state how many units are occupied at filing or how many will remain occupied during the work. Is that omission acceptable?

findings.reviewNote: Correct three required counts, greater-than-three threshold, application to 20 units, and amendment before occupancy. A repair added the unresolved actual counts; the tenant-protection-plan paragraph broadens the response.

cases.title: Permit with no work started for fourteen months
cases.question: DOB issued a construction permit fourteen months ago, but no work has begun. The permit was not otherwise renewed or preserved by a special provision. Is it still valid merely because the printed permit has not been physically surrendered?

findings.note: The explicit no-work premise is now accepted and the 14-versus-12-month expiration result is correct on the stated assumptions, without a rewrite. The answer still lists flood-hazard status as missing even though the scenario excludes special preservation. Keep that qualification from reopening the assumed scope.

cases.title: Owner’s duty to maintain an old building
cases.question: An owner argues that a deteriorated required building safeguard does not have to be maintained because the building is old and was lawfully constructed decades ago. Does the age of the building eliminate the owner’s maintenance obligation?

findings.note: Ongoing maintenance duty is correctly stated after a rewrite. Final wording still reopens whether the stated required safeguard is in fact required. The scenario already supplies that premise.

cases.title: Permit obtained through a material false statement
cases.question: DOB later discovers that a permit application contained a material false statement that affected issuance of the permit. Can the permit be revoked even though construction has already started?

findings.finding: Correct material-false-statement revocation authority despite construction commencement, notice and response opportunity. A full revision replaced mailed with the supplied provision wording posting of notice by mail. No automatic web search occurred.

cases.title: Unapproved alternative material
cases.question: A manufacturer submits a new construction material that appears stronger and more durable than the prescriptive material named in the code. Can the project use it immediately because the design team believes it is superior?

findings.note: Alternative method/material requires prior commissioner approval and the specified scope/equivalence conditions.

cases.title: Concealing work before required inspection
cases.question: The contractor wants to close a wall before a required DOB inspection because photographs were taken of the concealed work. Can the photographs substitute for keeping the work accessible for inspection?

findings.note: Work must remain accessible and exposed until the required inspection; photographs are not an automatic substitute.

cases.title: Satisfactory inspection as approval of a code violation
cases.question: DOB performed an inspection and marked it satisfactory. The design team later discovers that one inspected condition does not comply with an applicable code requirement. Does the satisfactory inspection make the noncompliant condition legal?

findings.finding: Correctly says a satisfactory inspection does not approve a violation. The final corrective-measure and enforcement discussion is unnecessary for this narrow question.

cases.title: Final inspection before work is complete
cases.question: A project requires a new or amended Certificate of Occupancy. The contractor asks DOB to perform the required final inspection while several items of permitted work are still incomplete so the Certificate of Occupancy process can start early. Is that the ordinary sequence allowed by the code?

findings.note: Final inspection follows completion of all permitted work and precedes the required certificate of occupancy. Extra address/amended-certificate survey context is explicitly conditional.

cases.title: Place of assembly operating with only a Certificate of Occupancy
cases.question: A room is legally classified as a place of assembly, and the building’s Certificate of Occupancy authorizes the assembly use. May the room operate without the required Place of Assembly Certificate of Operation?

findings.note: Certificate of occupancy does not replace the place-of-assembly certificate. Indoor/outdoor thresholds and the distinct temporary certificate remain bounded.

cases.title: Occupancy before a required Certificate of Occupancy
cases.question: Construction is complete and the project has passed its inspections, but the required Certificate of Occupancy has not yet been issued. Can the owner occupy the building because the physical work is finished?

findings.note: Correct central requirement for an issued occupancy certificate, but the exception discussion was bound only to AC 28-118.1. The verifier required the separate temporary/interim/partial authorities; the per-turn reservation blocked a complete rewrite.

cases.title: Continuing work after a stop-work order
cases.question: DOB issues a stop-work order that does not identify any portion of the project as permitted to continue. The contractor believes interior work in another area is unrelated to the cited violation. May that work continue?

findings.note: Correct all-work-stop conclusion with the commissioner danger-removal exception. Revision binds both the scope and continuation provisions to the contractor-belief point. Additional rescission rules are conditional.

cases.title: One toilet facility for a 28-person café
cases.question: A small café has a total occupant load of 28 people, including employees and customers. The required fixture count can be satisfied with one single-user toilet room. Must separate male and female toilet facilities still be provided?

findings.reviewNote: The combined employee/public condition, 28-versus-30 exception and accepted fixture-count premise are correct. Supported point 3 combines fixture credit with all-sexes signage but binds only PC 403.1.3; the signage clause belongs to PC 403.4. A separate correctly bound signage point and top-level citation do not fix that mixed-source point. Remove the duplicate or bind both sources.

cases.title: Drinking fountain in a restaurant that serves water
cases.question: A restaurant provides drinking water to customers as part of normal service. Does the Plumbing Code still require a separate drinking fountain solely because Table 403.1 would otherwise call for one?

findings.reviewNote: The restaurant water-service exception is applied directly, the ordinary table rate is accurately distinguished, and the answer avoids imposing unrelated drinking-fountain substitution requirements or requesting proof of the stated water service.

cases.title: Replacing all required drinking fountains with bottle fillers
cases.question: A building is required to provide four drinking fountains. The designer proposes four bottle-filling stations and no drinking fountains. Is that permitted?

findings.reviewNote: The answer preserves the 50-percent limit, two-fountain/two-filler result, faucet-height and adjacency/visibility conditions, and prohibition on bottled-water dispenser substitution in its supporting point. The standalone third paragraph and repeated compliant-layout description should be consolidated.

cases.title: Central apartment laundry without a floor drain
cases.question: A multiple-family residential building has a common laundry room with several automatic clothes washers, but the design omits a floor drain because each washer has a trapped standpipe. Is the floor drain optional?

findings.note: Central multiple-family laundry floor drain requirement is applied; standpipes do not substitute. Drainage of the entire floor, 3-inch outlet and lint strainer are retained.

cases.title: Commercial food-waste disposer without DEP approval
cases.question: A restaurant kitchen proposes a commercial food-waste disposer connected to the sanitary system. The disposer is a listed product, but no DEP approval has been obtained. Is the listing enough?

findings.reviewNote: Correctly cites PC 413.3 for DEP approval and distinguishes domestic listing rules. Domestic product standards, cold-water supply and approval-process caveats can be reduced.

cases.title: Cold water only at a public restroom lavatory
cases.question: A public restroom for customers is designed with cold water only at the hand-washing lavatories. Is that compliant?

findings.note: Public customer lavatory requires tempered water with the cited temperature-limiting provision. Point-of-use-heater exception does not make cold-only service sufficient.

cases.title: 30-inch-by-30-inch shower with a 20-inch entry
cases.question: A standard shower compartment is 30 inches by 30 inches internally, for 900 square inches of area, but its clear entry opening is only 20 inches wide. Does it satisfy the ordinary shower-compartment dimensional rules?

findings.note: A 30-by-30-inch ordinary compartment meets the 900-square-inch minimum; a 20-inch opening fails the 22-inch requirement. Finished dimensions, height and accessible-shower scope remain distinct.

cases.title: Replacing 75 percent of men’s water closets with urinals
cases.question: A men’s toilet room is required to provide four water closets. The designer proposes one water closet and three urinals. Can 75 percent of the required water closets be replaced by urinals?

findings.reviewNote: The 50-percent cap is applied to four required closets, yielding at most two substituted urinals. The proposed 75-percent replacement is rejected with a clear two-water-closet minimum and direct source support.

cases.title: Shower valve set to 125°F
cases.question: A pressure-balancing shower valve is field-adjusted so the maximum outlet temperature is 125°F. Is that setting permitted?

findings.note: 125 degrees F exceeds the 120-degree shower delivery limit by 5 degrees.

cases.title: Water heater above a finished office without a drain pan
cases.question: A storage-type water heater is installed above a finished office ceiling. Leakage from the heater could damage the ceiling and occupied space below, but no drain pan is shown. Is a pan required?

findings.note: Damage-risk tank heater requires a pan. Material, depth and drain dimensions are preserved. Replacement exception is limited to the drain with a leak detector; it does not remove the pan requirement.

cases.title: Three-inch sanitary piping at 1/16 inch per foot
cases.question: A new 3-inch horizontal sanitary drainage pipe is designed at a slope of 1/16 inch per foot. Is that enough?

findings.note: A 3-inch pipe requires 1/8 inch per foot; 1/16 is insufficient. Larger-pipe alternative is distinguished.

cases.title: Reducing a drain from four inches to three inches downstream
cases.question: A horizontal sanitary drain is 4 inches upstream but is reduced to 3 inches farther downstream in the direction of flow to avoid a beam. Is that permitted if the calculated fixture-unit load would fit in a 3-inch pipe?

findings.finding: Correctly applies the downstream no-reduction rule and identifies the specific water-closet connection exception. Repeats the result, but remains within scope.

cases.title: Double-trapping a sink
cases.question: A designer places two traps in series on a sink waste line to provide “extra protection” against sewer gas. Is double trapping permitted?

findings.note: Double trapping is prohibited. Additional single-trap arrangement exceptions are unnecessary to this decision but do not reverse it.

cases.title: Two-inch trap arm ten feet from the vent
cases.question: A fixture has a 2-inch trap arm with a developed length of 10 feet from the trap weir to the vent connection. No special venting method or exception is identified. Is that length permitted?

findings.note: A 10-foot trap arm exceeds the stated 8-foot allowance for the 2-inch case. The self-siphoning-fixture exception is not assumed.

cases.title: Basement fixtures subject to sewer backflow
cases.question: Basement plumbing fixtures are located at an elevation where they are subject to backflow from the public sewer, but the sanitary design provides no backwater valve. Is that acceptable?

findings.reviewNote: Correct accessible backwater protection and permitted fixture/branch/building-drain locations; no imported ban on the building-drain arrangement. Flood-area qualification is conditional.
